description: Synchronisation primitives decomposed. Futex's user-space fast path + kernel slow path. RCU (Read-Copy-Update) for lock-free reads. Sequence locks (seqlock) for write-rare data. Linux's wait queues. The mechanisms that make modern Linux mutex/semaphore/condvar fast.

sub_mechanisms.name: futex_uncontended_path
sub_mechanisms.definition: Atomic CAS on a user-space integer. On success (acquire) or release, no kernel involvement.
sub_mechanisms.why: ~10 ns per op vs ~µs for syscall. 99%+ of lock operations in well-designed code are uncontended. The 'fast path' is essentially free.

sub_mechanisms.name: FUTEX_WAIT
sub_mechanisms.definition: syscall: 'sleep until value at addr changes'. Kernel adds caller to per-address wait queue, sleeps.
sub_mechanisms.why: Contended case. Thread can't make progress; blocks in kernel. Cheaper than active spinning (CPU not wasted). The expensive but correct path when contention happens.

sub_mechanisms.name: FUTEX_WAKE
sub_mechanisms.definition: syscall: 'wake N waiters on this address'. Kernel removes them from wait queue, marks runnable.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lock release wakes waiting threads. N=1: wake one (avoids thundering herd). N=∞: broadcast (condition variable's signal-all).

sub_mechanisms.name: pthread_mutex_via_futex
sub_mechanisms.definition: User-space mutex_t holds a 32-bit state. Fast path: atomic CAS. Slow path: FUTEX_WAIT/WAKE on the state.
sub_mechanisms.why: Implementations the same shape: glibc, musl, every modern Linux mutex. Uncontended ~10ns; contended ~few µs. PI-mutex variant supports priority inheritance via FUTEX_LOCK_PI.

sub_mechanisms.name: RCU_read_copy_update
sub_mechanisms.definition: Lock-free read pattern: readers proceed without locking. Writers create new copy, swap pointer atomically, free old after grace period.
sub_mechanisms.why: Read-heavy data structures (RCU lists, rcu_dereference). Readers pay near-zero cost. Writers more expensive but rare. Linux kernel uses extensively (route tables, FS dentries, kernel data structures).

sub_mechanisms.name: RCU_grace_period
sub_mechanisms.definition: Time after which all currently-running readers have finished. Writers wait for grace period before freeing old data.
sub_mechanisms.why: Readers may still hold pointers to old version. Free before grace period ends = use-after-free. Linux's tree RCU + preemptible RCU detect grace periods efficiently.

sub_mechanisms.name: seqlock
sub_mechanisms.definition: Sequence lock: writer increments counter to odd (lock), modifies, increments to even (unlock). Reader: read counter; read data; read counter again; if same + even, valid.
sub_mechanisms.why: Optimised for write-rare data. Readers don't block writers; writers don't block readers. Cost: readers retry on race. Used in Linux for timekeeping (gettimeofday is seqlock-protected).

sub_mechanisms.name: wait_queue
sub_mechanisms.definition: Kernel data structure: list of threads waiting for an event. Threads add themselves + sleep; event-source wakes one or all.
sub_mechanisms.why: Generic blocking mechanism. Used by: futex, condition variables, completion, mutex contention. Each thread has wait_queue_entry; lists are doubly-linked for O(1) add/remove.

sub_mechanisms.name: completion
sub_mechanisms.definition: Kernel primitive: one thread waits for another to signal completion. complete() wakes; wait_for_completion() blocks.
sub_mechanisms.why: Single-event signalling. Like a one-shot condition variable. Used for I/O completion, thread synchronisation. complete_all() wakes everyone.

sub_mechanisms.name: memory_barrier_in_locks
sub_mechanisms.definition: Lock acquire = acquire barrier (no later read/write reorders before). Lock release = release barrier (no earlier read/write reorders after).
sub_mechanisms.why: Without barriers, compiler or CPU might reorder operations across the lock. Critical section's writes wouldn't be visible to next acquirer. Barriers in lock primitives enforce ordering.

sub_mechanisms.name: elision_lock_elision
sub_mechanisms.definition: Hardware feature (Intel TSX) speculatively skipping lock acquisition. If no conflict observed, commit without locking.
sub_mechanisms.why: Optimistic concurrency: most critical sections don't actually conflict. Hardware tracks accesses; aborts on conflict, retries with lock. Effective on read-heavy contended workloads. Has had security issues (Intel disabled TSX in some CPUs).

sub_mechanisms.name: MCS_lock
sub_mechanisms.definition: Scalable spinlock: each waiter spins on its own local node, not on a shared variable. Waiters form a queue.
sub_mechanisms.why: Avoids cache-line bouncing under contention. Each waiter waits on its own cache line (local spin). FIFO order — no starvation. Used in Linux's qspinlock + Java's biased locks.

derivation_rules.name: futex_amortises_kernel_cost_to_contention
if: a lock is acquired/released without contention
then: operation cost is user-space atomic only
derivation_rules.why: No syscall in uncontended path. The cost is 1 atomic operation (~10 ns). Kernel involved only when contention forces waiting. Pre-futex linux locks always entered kernel — ~100x slowdown.

derivation_rules.name: RCU_zero_cost_readers
if: readers operate via rcu_dereference + memory barrier
derivation_rules.why: Read path: load pointer + barrier. No locks, no atomics, no kernel. Writers carry the cost via copy + grace period wait. Read-heavy data structures (1000:1 read:write) make RCU essentially free for reads.

derivation_rules.name: seqlock_no_writer_block_at_reader_retry_cost
then: readers proceed lock-free at small retry cost
derivation_rules.why: Readers don't block writers; writers don't block readers. Reader cost: read + read + compare (~30 ns). Retry probability is low for write-rare data. Linux's gettimeofday optimised this way.

derivation_rules.name: MCS_eliminates_lock_cacheline_bouncing
if: many waiters spin on a single lock variable
then: the cache line bounces under contention
derivation_rules.why: Every waiter's spin loads the lock variable. Acquirer's release invalidates everyone's cached copy. MCS gives each waiter its own variable to spin on. Linux's qspinlock incorporates MCS — fixes scalability beyond ~16 cores.

derivation_rules.name: acquire_release_barriers_required_for_lock_correctness
if: a lock implementation lacks acquire/release barriers
then: operations in critical section may leak out
derivation_rules.why: Without acquire barrier, reads inside section may be reordered to before the acquire (seeing stale data). Without release, writes inside may be reordered to after release (next acquirer sees stale). Standard C++ atomic ordering models formalize.
